questions.question_text: How does the graph of $y=(x-4)^{2}(x+1)$ behave at the point $(4,0)$?

options.text: It touches the $x$-axis and turns back without crossing.
It cuts straight through the $x$-axis at an angle.
options.why: This is the behaviour at a zero of multiplicity $1$; here the multiplicity is $2$.

options.text: It flattens along the $x$-axis and crosses it.
options.why: Flattening while crossing needs an odd multiplicity of at least $3$.

options.text: It approaches the $x$-axis without ever reaching it.
options.why: A polynomial has no asymptotes, and $P(4)=0$ so the curve does meet the axis.

questions.question_text: At which $x$-intercept does the graph of $y=(x+1)^{2}(x-2)^{3}$ flatten along the $x$-axis as it crosses?

options.why: That zero has multiplicity $2$, so the curve touches the axis there rather than crossing.
Sign error: the factor $(x-2)^{3}$ gives the zero $x=2$, not $x=-2$.
Sign error: the factor $(x+1)^{2}$ gives the zero $x=-1$, and that zero touches anyway.
A multiplicity of $1$ would cut straight through, but the curve turns back at $x=-3$.
A multiplicity of $3$ would flatten and cross; it would also use up the whole degree, leaving no zero at $x=1$.
A multiplicity of $0$ would mean $x=-3$ is not a zero, yet the curve meets the axis there.

questions.solution_text:
The curve touches the axis at $x=-3$ and turns back, so that multiplicity is even.
The curve cuts straight through at $x=1$, so that multiplicity is $1$.
The multiplicities add to the degree $3$, so the multiplicity at $x=-3$ is $2$.

options.why: A multiplicity of $2$ at $x=1$ would touch and turn back, and the multiplicities would add to $3$, not $4$.
The curve cuts straight through at $x=-2$, so that multiplicity is odd, not even.
The flattening is at $x=1$, not at $x=-2$; the two multiplicities have been swapped.

questions.solution_text:
At $x=-2$ the curve cuts straight through, so that multiplicity is $1$.
At $x=1$ the curve flattens along the axis and crosses, so that multiplicity is odd and at least $3$.
$1+3=4$, which matches the degree.

options.why: Solved $4k=8$ instead of $4k=-8$, dropping the sign of the $y$-intercept; this curve passes through $(0,8)$ and rises as $x\to\infty$, not falls.
Made both slips at once: put the squared factor on the zero the curve cuts, and took $k=2$ from $4k=8$; this graph touches at $x=-1$ and rises as $x\to\infty$.
Attached the squared factor to the zero the curve cuts rather than the one it touches, carrying $k=-2$ across; this graph touches at $x=-1$, and at $x=0$ it gives $4$, not $-8$.

questions.solution_text:
The curve touches at $x=2$, so $(x-2)^{2}$ is a factor, and it cuts at $x=-1$, so $(x+1)$ is a factor.
$y=k(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$
$-8=k(0-2)^{2}(0+1)$
$-8=4k$
$k=-2$
$y=-2(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$

options.why: Counted one factor per intercept and ignored that each touching zero is repeated.
Gave only one of the two zeroes an even multiplicity; both must be even to touch.
An odd degree makes the two ends of the curve go in opposite directions, so the curve would have to cross the axis.

questions.solution_text:
Touching at $x=-1$ needs an even multiplicity, so the least is $2$.
Touching at $x=2$ needs an even multiplicity, so the least is $2$.
$2+2=4$, so the least possible degree is $4$.

options.why: Sign error in $k$: $y=k(27)(-1)=-27k=54$ gives $k=-2$.
The signs inside the brackets are reversed, giving intercepts at $3$ and $-1$.
Two double zeroes would touch the axis twice; the curve crosses at both intercepts shown.

questions.solution_text:
Flattening while crossing at $x=-3$ needs an odd multiplicity of at least $3$, and cutting at $x=1$ needs multiplicity $1$.
$3+1=4$, which matches the degree, so there are no other zeroes.
$y=k(x+3)^{3}(x-1)$
$54=k(3)^{3}(-1)$
$54=-27k$
$k=-2$
$y=-2(x+3)^{3}(x-1)$
